mathleague-2012-13-g5-01.title: Remove whole weeks
mathleague-2012-13-g5-01.body:
$18 = 14 + 4$. Fourteen days before Saturday is also a Saturday. Four more days before that: Friday, Thursday, Wednesday, Tuesday.

**Answer: (A) Tuesday**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-01.title: Count forward instead
mathleague-2012-13-g5-01.body:
Going back 18 days is like going back 21 days (3 weeks, still Saturday) and then forward 3 days: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday.

**Answer: (A) Tuesday**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-03.title: Number the songs
mathleague-2012-13-g5-03.body:
The songs before are numbers 1–6, the current one is number 7, and the 6 after are 8–13. That is 13 songs.

**Answer: (C) 13**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-04.title: Count tens
mathleague-2012-13-g5-04.body:
One hundred is 10 tens, so 100 hundreds is 1000 tens. $1000$ tens $\div$ $10$ tens $= 100$.

**Answer: (B) 100**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-06.title: Divide
mathleague-2012-13-g5-06.body:
3 characters per game and 30 characters in all: $30 \div 3 = 10$ games.

**Answer: (A) 10**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-07.title: Need an odd number of sides
mathleague-2012-13-g5-07.body:
A hexagon has 6 sides (even). Even + odd = odd, so the other shape needs an odd number of sides. A pentagon has 5: $6 + 5 = 11$, odd.

**Answer: (C) pentagon**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-07.title: Check each
mathleague-2012-13-g5-07.body:
Rhombus, square and quadrilateral all have 4 sides: $6 + 4 = 10$ is even. Pentagon: $6 + 5 = 11$ is odd.

**Answer: (C) pentagon**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-08.title: Watch out for left-to-right
mathleague-2012-13-g5-08.body:
Working left to right without the order of operations would give 1400 or 0 — those are traps. Multiplication comes first, giving 640.

**Answer: (C) 640**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-09.title: Take away the difference
mathleague-2012-13-g5-09.body:
Take the 6 extra years away from the sum: $30 - 6 = 24$ is twice my age, so I am 12. My brother is $12 + 6 = 18$.

**Answer: (C) 18**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-09.title: Try the choices
mathleague-2012-13-g5-09.body:
If my brother is 18, I am 12, and $18 + 12 = 30$ ✓.

**Answer: (C) 18**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-11.title: Compute
mathleague-2012-13-g5-11.body:
One dozen is 12 and two dozen is 24. $(12 + 24) \div 2 = 36 \div 2 = 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-11.title: Halfway
mathleague-2012-13-g5-11.body:
The average of two numbers is halfway between them; halfway between 1 and 2 dozen is $1\frac{1}{2}$ dozen $= 18$.

**Answer: (B) 18**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-12.title: Minutes, then halve
mathleague-2012-13-g5-12.body:
1 hour 46 minutes = $60 + 46 = 106$ minutes. Twice as fast takes half the time: $106 \div 2 = 53$ minutes.

**Answer: (A) 53**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-12.title: Halve each part
mathleague-2012-13-g5-12.body:
Half of 1 hour is 30 minutes and half of 46 minutes is 23 minutes: $30 + 23 = 53$.

**Answer: (A) 53**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-14.title: Subtract
mathleague-2012-13-g5-14.body:
The 4 schools have $4 \times 234 = 936$ students. The others have $2013 - 936 = 1077$.

**Answer: (A) 1077**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-14.title: Estimate first
mathleague-2012-13-g5-14.body:
$4 \times 234$ is a bit less than $4 \times 250 = 1000$, so the rest is a bit more than 1013 — only 1077 is close. Exactly: $2013 - 936 = 1077$.

**Answer: (A) 1077**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-15.title: List them
mathleague-2012-13-g5-15.body:
Call the books A, B, C: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA. That is 6 orders.

**Answer: (D) 6**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-15.title: Multiply choices
mathleague-2012-13-g5-15.body:
3 choices for the first spot, 2 for the second, 1 for the last: $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$.

**Answer: (D) 6**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-16.title: Find the new side
mathleague-2012-13-g5-16.body:
Twice the perimeter is 72 cm. Each side is $72 \div 4 = 18$ cm, so the area is $18 \times 18 = 324$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (D) 324 cm²**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-16.title: Scale the small square
mathleague-2012-13-g5-16.body:
The first square has side $36 \div 4 = 9$ cm and area 81 cm$^2$. Doubling the side multiplies the area by $2 \times 2 = 4$: $81 \times 4 = 324$ cm$^2$.

**Answer: (D) 324 cm²**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-17.title: Sets of three coins
mathleague-2012-13-g5-17.body:
One quarter, one dime and one nickel are worth $25 + 10 + 5 = 40$¢. So the total must be a multiple of 40¢. 240, 440 and 520 are multiples of 40, but $380 \div 40 = 9.5$ is not.

**Answer: (B) \$3.80**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-18.title: Factor pairs
mathleague-2012-13-g5-18.body:
12 = 1×12 = 2×6 = 3×4 gives three pairs (6 factors). 16 = 1×16 = 2×8 = 4×4 gives only 5 different factors; 6 and 9 have fewer.

**Answer: (C) 12**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-19.title: Find both
mathleague-2012-13-g5-19.body:
Multiples of 24: 24, 48, 72, 96, 120 — and 120 is the first that is a multiple of 10, so the LCM is 120. The GCF of 10 and 24 is 2. $120 + 2 = 122$.

**Answer: (B) 122**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-19.title: Use LCM × GCF = product
mathleague-2012-13-g5-19.body:
For two numbers, LCM × GCF = product: $10 \times 24 = 240$. The GCF is 2, so the LCM is $240 \div 2 = 120$. Sum: 122.

**Answer: (B) 122**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-20.title: Groups of 8
mathleague-2012-13-g5-20.body:
Each group of 5 cars and 3 trucks has 8 vehicles. $120 \div 8 = 15$ groups, so there are $15 \times 5 = 75$ cars.

**Answer: (C) 75**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-21.title: Change both units
mathleague-2012-13-g5-21.body:
600 m = 60 000 cm, so the rate is 60 000 cm per minute = 60 000 cm per 60 seconds. $60\,000 \div 60 = 1000$ cm/sec.

**Answer: (C) 1000**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-21.title: Seconds first
mathleague-2012-13-g5-21.body:
600 m per minute is $600 \div 60 = 10$ m per second, and 10 m = 1000 cm.

**Answer: (C) 1000**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-22.title: Count the overlap
mathleague-2012-13-g5-22.body:
$28 - 4 = 24$ dreams involved animals. Counting monkey dreams and squirrel dreams gives $16 + 15 = 31$, which is 7 more than 24. Those extra counts must be dreams counted twice, so at least 7 involved both.

**Answer: (B) 7**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-22.title: Make the overlap small
mathleague-2012-13-g5-22.body:
To make the overlap as small as possible, suppose every animal dream had a monkey or a squirrel. Of the 24 animal dreams, 16 have monkeys, leaving at most 8 without monkeys. The 15 squirrel dreams can use at most those 8, so at least $15 - 8 = 7$ squirrel dreams also have monkeys.

**Answer: (B) 7**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-23.title: Rule out the others
mathleague-2012-13-g5-23.body:
- Triangle: $3 + 3 < 8$, so a triangle with sides 3, 3, 8 cannot close.
- Square: all sides are equal.
- Parallelogram: opposite sides are equal, but the 1st and 3rd of three consecutive sides are 3 and 8.

A trapezoid can have sides 3, 3, 8 and a fourth side (e.g. 4).

**Answer: (D) trapezoid**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-23.title: Build one
mathleague-2012-13-g5-23.body:
Draw a bottom side of length 8. At its right end, go straight up 3. Then go left 3, parallel to the bottom. Joining back to the start of the bottom side closes a four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides — a trapezoid. Going around it, three consecutive sides are 3, 3 and 8.

**Answer: (D) trapezoid**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-24.title: Use the remainder
mathleague-2012-13-g5-24.body:
$500 = 6 \times 83 + 2$. The amounts left are always 2 more than a multiple of 6: 494, 488, ..., 14, 8, 2. Of the choices, only 8 ($6 + 2$) is on the list — it is what is left at the end of day 82.

**Answer: (B) 8**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-25.title: Compare costs
mathleague-2012-13-g5-25.body:
With 3 rides, "per ride" costs \$12.50 + \$15 = \$27.50, cheaper than \$30. With 4 rides it costs \$12.50 + \$20 = \$32.50, more than \$30. So at least 4 rides.

**Answer: (B) 4**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-25.title: Money left for rides
mathleague-2012-13-g5-25.body:
\$30 − \$12.50 = \$17.50 buys $17.50 \div 5 = 3.5$ rides. Once you take more than 3.5 rides — that is, 4 or more — the combo is cheaper.

**Answer: (B) 4**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-26.title: Find a 10
mathleague-2012-13-g5-26.body:
The product contains $5 \times 4 = 20$, a multiple of 10. So the whole product is a multiple of 10 and ends in 0.

**Answer: (A) 0**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-26.title: 5 times an even number
mathleague-2012-13-g5-26.body:
Any product with a factor 5 and an even factor ends in 0. Here we have 5 and 8 (and more).

**Answer: (A) 0**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-27.title: Totals
mathleague-2012-13-g5-27.body:
First 4 games: $4 \times 31 = 124$ points. First 5 games: $5 \times 30 = 150$ points. Game 5: $150 - 124 = 26$.

**Answer: (A) 26**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-27.title: Balance around 30
mathleague-2012-13-g5-27.body:
Each of the first 4 games was 1 point above 30 on average, 4 points extra in all. For the 5-game average to be exactly 30, game 5 must be 4 below 30: 26.

**Answer: (A) 26**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-28.title: List them
mathleague-2012-13-g5-28.body:
Listing by where the first X is:
- XOXOXOO, XOXOOXO, XOXOOOX, XOOXOXO, XOOXOOX, XOOOXOX
- OXOXOXO, OXOXOOX, OXOOXOX
- OOXOXOX

That is 10 orders.

**Answer: (D) 10**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-28.title: Gaps between the O's
mathleague-2012-13-g5-28.body:
Write the 4 O's: _O_O_O_O_. There are 5 gaps, and each X goes into a different gap (so no two X's touch). Choosing 3 of the 5 gaps is the same as choosing 2 gaps to leave empty: the pairs from 5 gaps are 1-2, 1-3, 1-4, 1-5, 2-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-4, 3-5, 4-5 — 10 ways.

**Answer: (D) 10**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-29.title: Add then subtract
mathleague-2012-13-g5-29.body:
Mo + Jo + Bo + Ko $= 120 + 153 = 273$. Removing Mo and Bo's 127 coins leaves Jo + Ko $= 273 - 127 = 146$.

**Answer: (D) 146**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-29.title: Example
mathleague-2012-13-g5-29.body:
We don't need each person's amount, but one example: Mo 100, Jo 20, Bo 27, Ko 126 fits all three facts, and Jo + Ko = 146.

**Answer: (D) 146**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-30.title: Make it long and thin
mathleague-2012-13-g5-30.body:
Putting all 100 squares in one row makes a 2-by-200 rectangle with perimeter $2 \times (2 + 200) = 404$. Any other arrangement (like 4 by 100 or 20 by 20) is less stretched out and has a smaller perimeter.

**Answer: (D) 404**

mathleague-2012-13-g5-30.title: Compare arrangements
mathleague-2012-13-g5-30.body:
Arranging the squares $a$ by $b$ (with $a \times b = 100$) gives a $2a$ by $2b$ rectangle with perimeter $4(a + b)$. The biggest $a + b$ is $1 + 100 = 101$, giving $4 \times 101 = 404$.

**Answer: (D) 404**
